## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## The respondents

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

screens.why5: The forwarding and PMS rows still mean what I typed, but the review turned my 'could forward' into a permission and recast my PMS line as an 'allowed to' row, a little away from my own words.
screens.why7: Forwarding is correctly a permission and the PMS row a fact true for some and not others, but the third row is a permission the agent never holds or sees and half-overlaps the PMS row, which bends the card's 'one thing to weigh, no two about the same thing' rule.
screens.instead: Keep 'Could have unanswered calls forwarded to another number (with the phone admin's OK)' and 'Ran OPERA Cloud, Sihot or Apaleo as their PMS', and drop the outside-software row or fold it into the PMS one.

screens.why1: After checking my conditions, picking the one to put to strangers is the obvious next step, and the bar beside it tells me what I am signing up for.
screens.why2: Call forwarding, PMS, OPERA Cloud, Sihot and Apaleo are everyday words at a German reservations office, so I can read every row first time (only the 'Were' / 'were' capitalisation is untidy).
screens.why3: Whether a hotel's calls can be forwarded and which PMS it runs is exactly what I sort out with every group I sign, so I can judge which is most likely missing.
screens.why4: The three rows are mostly distinct, but Keel's suggestion (outside software writing into the PMS) and my PMS row both test whether we can plug into the PMS, so two rows overlap.
screens.why5: I typed 'could forward unanswered calls to another number', and the review turned it into 'were allowed to have ... forwarded'; what actually stops a hotel is usually an old phone system that cannot forward, not a missing permission, so the meaning has drifted a little.
screens.why7: The picked row is one act, not settled by my segment, and served as a permission with a bar of 1 in 3 against, so the belief can hold or fail; but Keel's suggested row and the PMS row are about the same integration, which bends the 'no two about the same thing' rule.
screens.instead: Which one do you want to test? -- Had a phone system that could forward unanswered calls to another number · Ran OPERA Cloud, Sihot or Apaleo as their PMS (Keel's suggestion: the PMS link is the step most likely missing)

screens.why1: Right after I said how it fits their day, asking what it does better than their way today (calling missed calls back when there's time) is the obvious next step in the solution section.
screens.why2: The question and hint are plain to me, and 'one benefit a line, up to four, each up to 9 words' told me exactly how to type 'Missed calls turned into bookings' and 'Callers answered when the desk is busy'.
screens.why3: What my AI does better than a central office that misses 5% of calls is the thing I pitch every day, so I can answer it straight from my own material.
screens.why4: The only chip is the escape 'I'm not sure', which fits a founder's answer box, and the free box let me write both benefits in my own words.
screens.why5: Nothing is rewritten here; my two benefits stand as I typed them, and the hint's framing ('what reservation agents would get that today's way does not give them') matches the job I set, turning every caller into a booking.
screens.why7: The box asks for what the card requires (1 to 4 benefits, each at most 9 words, each against today's way, with 'I'm not sure' as the founder's escape), and my two rows are distinct noun phrases with no number I didn't write.

screens.why1: Right after I typed what Codyco does better, this is where I check Keel's rows before they become the belief, so it sits exactly where I expect it.
screens.why2: "Missed calls turned into bookings" and "callers answered when the desk is busy" are how my reservations people and I talk; nothing needs a second read.
screens.why3: Both rows are about calls my agents see ring out on their own shifts, so they are things they know from their week.
screens.why4: The two rows overlap: a caller answered when the desk is busy is mostly how a missed call becomes a booking, so they are one gain told twice, and the after-hours and holiday calls I lead with have no row of their own.
screens.why5: My point was after hours, at peak and on holidays, and "when the desk is busy" keeps only the peak, so the meaning has drifted a little toward the rush.
screens.why7: The belief carries both rows joined with "and" against the study's hard case, so the four-rung scale can still support or refute it, but the rows overlap rather than being distinct gains, and one unanswered call "giving them missed calls" (plural) bends the belief's sense.
screens.instead: Rows: "Every booking call answered, day, night or holiday" · "The booking written straight into the PMS" -- so the belief reads: their last reservation call that rang out unanswered would have been answered and booked straight into the PMS.

screens.why1: Right after I said what Codyco does better, asking what my reservation agents have to do to start with it is the obvious next question about the idea.
screens.why2: 'What will they have to do to start using it' with 'setup, extra steps or learning' is plain to me, and nine words a row is easy to keep to.
screens.why3: I know exactly what the desk and the central office have to do: let the missed calls go to the AI and pick up what it passes back.
screens.why4: It is a box to type in; the only chip is 'I'm not sure', which is the right way out for a founder who cannot name the effort.
screens.why5: My two rows came through as I meant them: handing over the missed booking calls and taking the calls the AI hands to the desk, both in 'their' voice.
screens.why7: The question and hint ask for the card's measure (setup, extra steps, learning) in up to four rows of nine words, and both my rows are efforts the agents take themselves, not a sign-off, a PMS fit or a purchase step, with the founder's 'I'm not sure' escape present.

screens.why1: Right after I said what agents must do to start, Keel shows the efforts it drafted for me to check, which is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Missed booking calls, the AI and calls handed to the desk are how my reservation agents talk; the intro only repeats the title, which costs nothing.
screens.why3: An agent knows whether they would let missed calls go to the AI and take the handovers on their shift.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts in my own words, both 'their' voice and under 9 words: letting go of the missed calls, and the new habit of taking the AI's handovers.
screens.why5: These are my two rows as I saved them; nothing drifted.
screens.why7: The second row is a clean new habit the agent takes on, but the first ('hand their missed booking calls to the AI') reads as much like the director's routing decision, and it brushes Compatibility's call-forwarding ground, so the agent's answer may say whether the group allows it rather than whether they'd take the effort.
screens.instead: Rows: Take every call the AI hands to the desk; Check the AI's bookings in the PMS each shift -- asked: you'd check the bookings it writes into your PMS on each shift.

screens.why1: After I listed what agents have to do to start, picking the one effort most likely to stop them is the obvious next step before the belief goes to strangers.
screens.why2: 'Missed booking calls', 'the AI' and 'the desk' are how my reservation agents talk on any shift, so both rows read at first glance.
screens.why3: Both efforts sit inside an agent's own day: letting the calls they would miss go to the AI, and taking the calls it passes back to them.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts, one giving calls away and one taking calls back, both in my words, with nothing nonsensical or doubled.
screens.why5: The rows are the two I kept, and the belief tests the one I picked: whether agents would hand their missed booking calls to the AI.
screens.why7: Each row is one effort the agents take themselves, a habit of use rather than another role's sign-off or a Compatibility or Purchase condition; there are 1 to 4 rows in 'their' voice, and the belief can be held or sunk by the stranger's Yes/Only if against Probably not/No.

screens.why1: Just before the study goes out is the right time to decide whether to collect people who want to try Codyco, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: 'Offer a pilot?' with 'Yes, ask them / No pilot' is plain to me, and the hint shows exactly the line respondents will see.
screens.why3: Whether I want a list of hotels to pilot with is my own decision, and running pilots is how I sell.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers the choice completely, and the two options are distinct and in my words.
screens.why5: My pilot is a paid €3,000 money-back trial at one hotel, agreed by the revenue director, but the screen offers a free-sounding 'leave your email' line to reservation agents, who cannot commit the group, so the meaning drifts a little.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? Respondents who say yes see: "Would your hotel try this at one location? Leave your email and we'll put you in touch with whoever decides." Options: Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Choosing who asks my questions belongs in the last step before the link goes out, after the pilot offer and before people see the study.
screens.why2: The question itself is plain, but the hint packs video, typing or tapping, a preselected voice, recording once, 400 credits and text messages into one paragraph, so I would read it twice.
screens.why3: I can play both samples and judge which voice my reservation agents in Munich would take seriously on a call-like video.
screens.why4: Two named voices with five-second samples is a clean choice, but nothing tells me whether either one speaks German to German reservation agents, and that is the one thing I would need to know.
screens.why5: Nothing of Codyco, the AI receptionist or the director's role leaks into this screen, and the respondents stay reservation agents.
screens.instead: Who should ask your reservation agents the questions, in German? Options: Daphne (German) ▶ 5 s / Saskia (German) ▶ 5 s, with the 400 credits on a separate line.

screens.why1: After choosing who asks the questions, how the reservation agents will answer is the natural next thing to settle before the study goes out.
screens.why2: Three short options in plain words; 'Daphne' is explained in its own line, so I read it once and know what each means.
screens.why3: I know my agents -- on a shift, between calls at a desk -- so I can judge whether they would rather tap through or talk to a video.
screens.why4: AI voice, text, or let them pick covers the real choices, none overlap, and each says plainly what the agent will do.
screens.why5: Nothing of Codyco or the director leaks; it speaks of reservation agents, in the words I typed.

screens.why1: After choosing how agents answer, the last step is who gets the link, so this screen fits where it sits at the end of sending interviews.
screens.why2: Three plain ways to reach people, by name, from a Keel search, or one open link in a group, and I can pick on first reading.
screens.why3: I know who I would send this to: the reservation agents and front-desk staff at our 7 hotel groups and their friends in the trade, so I can answer from my own work.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and cover my real cases, but the Keel search option names a 'Contacts page' I have not seen anywhere in this flow, and nothing says whether I can mix named people with an open link.
screens.why5: Nothing about Codyco, the AI or the pilot leaks into this sending screen, and my pick (people I know by name) is kept as I typed it.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? -- People I know by name (I send each their own link) / People Keel finds for me (pick a list, Keel makes a link for each) / A group, one open link (post it where agents already talk, e.g. a hotel-staff WhatsApp group) -- and allow more than one.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits under the title and the tally '3 beliefs: 3 holding · 7 people answered' with each card's count against its bar (6 of 7, 5 of 7, 6 of 7 vs bar 5 of 7) decides it right beside it.
screens.why_b2: The stage page draws no chart, but each card's count line says what was counted, over 7 people and where the bar sits; 'at the bar' and '3 on a condition' need a second look to read as weak spots.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and Adoption friction are my beliefs in my words, but the statement has a doubled 'the hotel the hotel' and a garbled ending, and the Relative advantage line is stitched awkwardly ('would have given them missed calls turned into bookings').
screens.why_b4: Saying the verdict is the worst of the cards tells me all three held, but nothing says concretely what to do next, such as go to the €3,000 pilot ask or firm up relative advantage, which only just made its bar.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and 'at the bar' is flagged, but 'Holding up' across the board with relative advantage exactly at 5 of 7 and three of six adopters conditional is a soft overstatement for seven people.
screens.instead: Holding up with 7 people, but only just: relative advantage sits exactly at the bar and half the adopters want conditions, so ask the next hotel groups for the paid pilot and hear those conditions before calling it settled.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 said yes, easily or with some steps · bar 5 of 7", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts each answer over 7 people, and the strip shows 6 for and 1 against with the marker at 5, so what is counted, out of how many, and where my bar sits are plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: I checked 'could forward unanswered calls to another number'; the card says 'were allowed to have unanswered calls forwarded'. I recognise it, but it is no longer my words, and 'You said were allowed to...' reads clipped.
screens.why_b4: The So line tells me forwarding is not the blocker and sends me to Adoption friction, which is a concrete next place to look.
screens.why_b5: The count line says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', but the So line flatly says this 'is not what will stop them' on 7 people. Aylin's quote shows her hotel's old phone system cannot forward at all, which is a technical blocker the permission wording hides.
screens.instead: Holding up, 6 of 7, a lean with only 7 people. Forwarding looks unlikely to stop most groups, but Aylin's old phone system cannot forward at all, so check each hotel's phone system before the pilot and look at Adoption friction next.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 5 of 7 better against a bar of 5 of 7, at the bar, so I know it held and by exactly how much.
screens.why_b2: Better 5 (all a lot), Same 1, Worse 1 over 7 people, with 2 of 7 against and the 1-in-3 bar marked at 5, reads at first look.
screens.why_b3: The name and the belief carry both my benefits, missed calls turned into bookings and callers answered when the desk is busy, though the You said line under it keeps only the first.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates 5 of 7 and points me to Adoption friction, but it never says what this means for Codyco, such as Chiara's group where a call center already covers after hours.
screens.why_b5: It says a small group, a lean not a call, keeps 7 visible and does not call a pass exactly at the bar strong.
screens.instead: Held, but only just: 5 of 7 said a lot better, and one more No difference would break the bar; the two against are a group whose call center already covers after hours and a desk that won't hand guests to a machine, so lead with groups without after-hours cover.

screens.why_b1: The verdict reads Holding up, and right beside it is the number that decides it: 6 of 7 would do it against a bar of 5 of 7, with the 3 on a condition named.
screens.why_b2: The bars count each answer, the 7 people show in the strip and the count line, and the marker at 5 sits where the rule says it should, so I read all three at first look.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and 'Most would hand their missed booking calls to the AI' are my words, though the bare 'You said hand their missed booking calls to the AI.' line reads like a fragment.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the split and points me 'below', where the list only repeats the condition, so it never tells me to prove that forwarded calls land as intact bookings in the PMS or what to make of the one firm No.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, the small group is flagged as 'a lean, not a call', and the conditional yeses are split out rather than folded into a plain yes, so nothing is overstated.
screens.instead: 3 of 7 would hand their missed calls over as is and 3 only if guests' bookings arrive intact, so show them a forwarded call landing as a correct booking in the PMS on the pilot, because one agent would not do it at all.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on "Holding up" with the deciding count beside it (6 of 7 against a bar of 5; 5 of 7 at the bar of 5), so I know both the verdict and the number behind it.
screens.why_b3: Both dimension names are mine, but the beliefs are reworded: Compatibility says "were allowed to have" calls forwarded where I checked whether they could forward them, and the Relative advantage line is a garbled stitch ("their last reservation call... would have given them missed calls turned into bookings") that I recognise but would not have written.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what to do next, for example budgeting IT help for old phone systems or treating groups with a 24h call center as a weaker segment; it only introduces the quotes.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 stays visible, but Relative advantage sits exactly at the bar on 7 people without being called thin, and "1 never saw it (Murat)" next to "6 of 7" leaves me unsure whether Murat is inside the 7 or outside it.
screens.why_b6: The quotes add things I never typed: forwarding can be blocked by an old phone system the owner won't pay to replace, some guests call to reach a person who knows the house, and where a call center already covers evenings the agent's real pain is group requests by email.

screens.why1: As the first screen it checks that I'm the right person before anything about my calls is asked, and I see why it's there.
screens.why2: Central reservations office and call center for a hotel group are the words we use for my own office in Munich, so I can answer it straight away.
screens.why3: I know where I work, so I can answer without guessing.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it with no overlap, and a screener needs no escape.
screens.why5: It names my workplace only, and nothing of a product or the founder's terms reaches me.
screens.why6: The question is easy to hear once, but 'I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No.' is a clumsy way to offer a yes-or-no when 'Yes or no?' would do.
screens.instead: Do you work in a central reservations office or call center for a hotel group in Germany? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I work in a central reservations office, asking whether a call went unanswered this week is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: I understand it at once, but 'did you have a call ring out' is odd for me: in our office calls sit in the queue and drop off as lost calls, so they are never one agent's own.
screens.why3: On a trade-fair Saturday I see the queue and the lost-call count on the board, but whether a call that rang out was 'mine' is something I'd have to guess, since the system routes them to whoever is free.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it and are distinct, and the chips belong to the story box after a Yes, not to the gate.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's unanswered booking call and names no product, plan or outside term for us.
screens.why6: It is one short sentence followed by 'Yes or no,' which is easy to answer after hearing it once.
screens.why7: It asks the costly event, a call nobody answered, rather than the routine of taking calls, so an agent whose queue was covered all week can truly say No and the share can hold or fail against the band.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did a booking call to your office go unanswered while you were on shift? Yes · No

screens.why1: I just said calls rang out unanswered last week, so being shown something that picks those calls up is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: PMS, OPERA Cloud, Sihot and Apaleo are the words of my desk, and the rest is plain, though 'your hotel' is a little off since I sit in the group's central office, not at one hotel.
screens.why3: Calls nobody picks up, forwarding, taking the card and the booking landing in the PMS are exactly what I deal with every shift.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It is clearly shown as an idea, and nothing reaches me that I would not expect from such a card; it means what it says.
screens.why6: Heard once, it runs seven sentences where the rule asks for three lines, and the fragment 'That is OPERA Cloud, Sihot or Apaleo' is a list of product names I have to catch in passing.
screens.instead: Imagine Codyco, an AI reservation agent that takes the calls nobody picks up. Unanswered calls go to it; it answers in your hotels' voice, takes the payment, books straight into your PMS, and passes calls to your desk by your rules. The people building it believe it would turn those missed calls into confirmed bookings.

screens.why1: Right after the Codyco card, asking whether the calls we miss could even reach it is the obvious next question for me.
screens.why2: Every word is plain to me, but 'were you allowed to have unanswered calls forwarded' needs a second read, because at our office overflow routing is set in the phone system by IT and the team lead, not something I am 'allowed' to do.
screens.why3: I know our calls go to the overflow queue, but whether forwarding to an outside number is permitted is the team lead's or IT's call, and tying it to my last booking call makes me guess about a standing setup, not that one call.
screens.why4: 'Yes, easily' and 'Yes, with some steps' are odd answers to 'were you allowed', and 'Yes, with some steps' overlaps with 'Only with help or approval', since my steps would be asking for approval.
screens.why5: I hear nothing of the founder's own terms beyond the idea card shown on purpose, and the condition still means forwarding the missed calls elsewhere.
screens.why6: Heard once, it is one short question with four short options I can hold and one escape said last.
screens.why7: It is a permission with the right four options in order and 'I can't tell' set apart, and it can go either way across offices, but the stem asks 'were you allowed to have' instead of the card's passive (could unanswered calls have been forwarded), so the graded yeses sit awkwardly on an allowed-or-not measure.
screens.instead: Think of your last booking call. Could a call nobody picked up have been forwarded to another number? Yes, easily; yes, with some steps; only with help or approval; no; or I can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, I see why I'm asked whether this AI would have helped with the calls we miss at peak, which is exactly what screen 2 asked me about.
screens.why2: 'Rang out before anyone answered' could mean it rang a long time and someone finally picked up, not that it went unanswered as screen 2 said, and 'done that better' makes me stop to work out what 'that' is.
screens.why3: On a trade-fair Saturday calls ring out at our office every hour, so I can judge from my own shift whether something picking them up would have helped.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover what I'd say, including worse if a guest hangs up on a machine, and 'I can't tell' fits.
screens.why5: Codyco is named only through the idea card shown on purpose, and 'reservation agent' is my own job title, so nothing slips in that I wouldn't say.
screens.why6: Heard once, it is two short sentences and four short options I can hold, then the escape, with nothing only the eye can read.
screens.why7: The card's four fixed answers are in order on one measure (better or not, and how much), it can be supported and refuted, and the hard case is the missed call with the one escape apart.
screens.instead: Think of the last booking call that rang out unanswered. Would Codyco, an AI reservation agent, have handled it better for you, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: After the idea card and the better-or-not question, asking whether I'd actually start letting it take our calls is the natural next step.
screens.why2: I get it on first hearing, but 'hand my missed calls to it' is vague for something that just rings out, and nobody in our office would say a booking stays 'intact'; we'd say it goes into the system correctly.
screens.why3: I know whether I'd trust it, but where calls overflow is set up by our team lead and the telephony people, not by me, so my answer is partly a guess at what I'd be allowed to do.
screens.why4: Yes, probably not, no and I can't tell are fine, but the 'Only if' condition is worded oddly; my real condition is that it books into our system correctly with the right rate and dates.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's plan leaks past the idea card, and the screen still means letting the AI take the calls nobody picks up.
screens.why6: It is short, one question, four short options I can hold, and one escape said last.
screens.why7: The options are on the one measure with a working for and against side and the right escape, but the effort is barely mine: a missed call needs no step from me, and the routing is our team lead's and IT's job, close to the forwarding question on screen 4 (Compatibility), so the rule that the step is the person's own is bent.
screens.instead: To use Codyco, you'd check the bookings it took in your system each shift. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Only if it enters rates and dates correctly · Probably not · No · I can't tell
